title: Quantum mechanics: formalism, experiment, and interpretations that do not agree

body:
## What was built, in order

Planck's 1901 paper states a law for the energy distribution of black-body radiation. That is a result about spectra, not yet a mechanics of atoms.

Schrödinger's 1926 papers, both titled *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem*, turn quantization into an eigenvalue problem for a wave function. Born's 1926 paper on collision processes is the statistical reading: the wave function is used to give probabilities. Heisenberg's 1927 paper is the uncertainty argument, about what the new kinematics allows one to mean by simultaneous values of quantities such as position and momentum.

Those papers are the machinery. They are not an agreement about what the machinery says the world is doing between measurements.

## What experiment has actually closed

Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen (1935) asked whether the quantum description is complete. Bell (1964) turned a version of that question into an inequality that local hidden-variable theories must satisfy. Aspect, Grangier, and Roger (1982) reported a violation of a Bell inequality in an optical experiment.

**Fact:** that class of local hidden-variable theories does not fit those results.

**Not settled:** which of the remaining interpretations is right. Everett's relative-state formulation and Bohm's hidden-variable theory are both published alternatives. Neither is selected by the Bell test alone. Calling one of them "the" meaning of quantum mechanics is an interpretation, not a further measurement.

## Mechanism, stated narrowly

The predictive mechanism that working physics uses is: write the wave function from Schrödinger's equation (or an equivalent formalism), and read probabilities from it in the way Born's rule specifies. The uncertainty paper limits how sharp a joint classical picture of the same system can be. Everything past that sentence — collapse, many branches, guiding waves — is a contested reading of the same predictions.

contested_views.label: The wave function is a probability tool, not a catalog of hidden positions
contested_views.summary: Born's 1926 paper treats the quantum description of collisions statistically. In the reading that became textbook quantum mechanics, the wave function is used to compute probabilities of outcomes, and Heisenberg's 1927 paper argues that the kinematics itself limits how sharp simultaneous values can be. This is an interpretation of the formalism plus an argument about measurement, not an extra experimental object.

contested_views.label: The description is incomplete unless extra variables exist
contested_views.summary: Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen (1935) argued that the quantum-mechanical description of physical reality is not complete. Bohm (1952) wrote an explicit hidden-variable interpretation. Bell (1964) then showed that a local hidden-variable account of the EPR setup has to obey inequalities. Aspect, Grangier, and Roger (1982) reported an experimental violation of a Bell inequality. That rules out a class of local hidden-variable theories. It does not by itself pick a single remaining interpretation.

contested_views.label: The wave function never collapses; branching relative states are enough
contested_views.summary: Everett's 1957 paper formulates quantum mechanics in terms of relative states, without adding a separate collapse postulate. Whether that formulation matches what an observer should expect is still argued. The paper is a real alternative, not a settled replacement.
